title: The strong law of large numbers
statement: \begin{gathered} X_1, X_2, \dots \ \text{i.i.d.}, \quad \mathbb{E}|X_1| < \infty \\ \Longrightarrow \ \bar X_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i \to \mathbb{E} X_1 \ \text{almost surely} \end{gathered}
assumptions: The X_i have the same law.
The X_i are pairwise independent (Etemadi). Full independence is the classical condition.
proof: Truncate: Y_k = X_k 1{|X_k| ≤ k}. Integrability gives Σ P(X_k ≠ Y_k) < ∞, so X_k = Y_k for all large k (Borel–Cantelli). Chebyshev's inequality on a geometric subsequence n_j = ⌊α^j⌋ with α > 1 gives almost sure convergence of the truncated means. For X ≥ 0, monotonicity covers the indices between the n_j. Then split X = X⁺ − X⁻.
reference: R. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Cambridge University Press, 2019, Theorem 2.4.1. N. Etemadi, An elementary proof of the strong law of large numbers, Z. Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie verw. Gebiete 55 (1981) 119–122.
counterexample: The zeta law with s = 1.8 has E[X] = ∞. Then X̄_n → ∞ almost surely, so no finite limit exists.

title: The central limit theorem and the CLT interval
assumptions: The X_i are i.i.d.
The variance σ² is finite and positive.
The coverage 0.95 of the interval X̄_n ± 1.96 s_n/√n is a limit as n → ∞. A bound for a given n needs more, for example E|X|³ < ∞ (Berry–Esseen).
proof: Let φ be the characteristic function of X_1 − μ. Then φ(u) = 1 − σ²u²/2 + o(u²), and the characteristic function of the normalised sum is φ(t/(σ√n))^n. Its limit is e^(−t²/2). Lévy's continuity theorem gives convergence in law. Slutsky's lemma replaces σ by s_n.
reference: R. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., 2019, Theorem 3.4.1. B. V. Gnedenko and A. N. Kolmogorov, Limit Distributions for Sums of Independent Random Variables, Addison-Wesley, 1954.
counterexample: The zeta law with s = 2.5 has a finite mean and an infinite variance. Then (S_n − nμ)/n^(2/3) converges in law to a stable law with index 1.5, not to a normal law. Thus the CLT interval has no coverage guarantee. The block coverage in the diagnostics shows the effect in a run.

title: Consistency of the estimator and exactness of rejection
assumptions: Each replicate draws exactly from the model law.
For rejection: p and q each sum to 1, and p(k) ≤ M q(k) for every k. The acceptance uniform is independent of the proposal.
proof: Unbiasedness follows from the linearity of expectation, and consistency from the strong law. For rejection, P(accept, Y = k) = q(k) p(k)/(M q(k)) = p(k)/M. The sum over k gives P(accept) = 1/M. Divide to get P(Y = k | accept) = p(k).
reference: L. Devroye, Non-Uniform Random Variate Generation, Springer, 1986, chapter II. S. Asmussen and P. W. Glynn, Stochastic Simulation: Algorithms and Analysis, Springer, 2007, chapter II.
counterexample: If M is too small, the accepted values follow min(p, Mq) after normalisation, not p. The estimator is then consistent for the wrong quantity.

title: Monte Carlo error and the zero-hit bound
assumptions: The replicates are independent.
σ_g² = Var g(X) is finite for Var θ̂_n = σ_g²/n.
For the zero-hit bound, each replicate shows the event independently with the same probability p.
proof: The variance of a sum of independent terms is the sum of their variances, so Var θ̂_n = σ_g²/n for any dimension of X. For the bound: P(0 hits) = (1 − p)^n, which is at most α if and only if p ≥ 1 − α^(1/n). Thus a test at level α rejects every p above the bound.
reference: S. Asmussen and P. W. Glynn, Stochastic Simulation, 2007, chapter III. J. A. Hanley and A. Lippman-Hand, If nothing goes wrong, is everything all right? JAMA 249 (1983) 1743–1745.
counterexample: If replicates reuse 16 streams, the draws repeat and are not independent. The formula s/√n then understates the error by a factor near √(n/16), and the intervals cover the reference less often.

title: Variance reduction: when each method lowers the variance
statement: \begin{gathered} \operatorname{Var}\hat\theta_{\mathrm{st}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_k w_k \sigma_k^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_k w_k (\mu_k - \mu)^2 \\ \operatorname{Var}\hat\theta_{\mathrm{av}} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}(1 + \rho), \quad \rho \le 0 \ \text{if} \ g \ \text{is monotone} \\ \min_{\beta} \operatorname{Var}(Y - \beta C) = \sigma_Y^2 \left(1 - \rho_{YC}^2\right) \\ \operatorname{Var}\left(Y^{(a)} - Y^{(b)}\right) = \sigma_a^2 + \sigma_b^2 - 2\operatorname{Cov}\left(Y^{(a)}, Y^{(b)}\right) \end{gathered}
assumptions: Stratification: the allocation n_k = w_k n is proportional to the exact stratum probabilities w_k.
Antithetic variables: X = F⁻¹(U) and X' = F⁻¹(1 − U), and g is non-decreasing or non-increasing in each uniform.
Control variates: 0 < Var C < ∞, Var Y < ∞, and μ_C is exact.
Common random numbers: the same uniforms drive both alternatives. The gain needs a positive covariance of the outputs.
proof: Stratification: the law of total variance splits σ² into the mean of the variances inside the strata and the variance of the stratum means. Proportional allocation removes the second part. Antithetic pairs: Var((Y + Y')/2) = (σ²/2)(1 + ρ) for one pair. If g is monotone, then one of g(U) and g(1 − U) increases with U and the other decreases. So their covariance is at most 0 (Chebyshev's association inequality). Control variates: Var(Y − βC) = σ_Y² − 2β Cov(Y, C) + β² Var C is smallest at β* = Cov(Y, C)/Var C, with the value σ_Y²(1 − ρ²). Common random numbers: the variance of a difference follows from the bilinearity of the covariance.
reference: S. Asmussen and P. W. Glynn, Stochastic Simulation: Algorithms and Analysis, Springer, 2007, chapter V. P. Glasserman, Monte Carlo Methods in Financial Engineering, Springer, 2004, chapter 4. A. B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, 2013, chapters 8 and 10.
counterexample: Let g be an even function of a symmetric input, such as (X − μ)² for a normal X. Then g(X') = g(X) for the antithetic partner X' = 2μ − X. Thus ρ = 1, and the pairs double the variance for the same number of evaluations.

title: Regular variation and subexponentiality
statement: \begin{gathered} \bar F(x) = x^{-\alpha}\ell(x), \ \ \frac{\ell(tx)}{\ell(x)} \to 1 \ (x \to \infty) \ \text{for every} \ t > 0 \ \ \Longrightarrow \\ \mathbb{P}(X_1 + \dots + X_n > x) \sim n\,\bar F(x) \sim \mathbb{P}\left(\max_{i \le n} X_i > x\right) \ \ (x \to \infty) \end{gathered}
assumptions: X_1, …, X_n are nonnegative and i.i.d. with the law F, for a fixed n.
The tail is regularly varying with an index α > 0: F̄(x) = x^(−α) ℓ(x) with ℓ slowly varying. Then F is subexponential.
A subexponential law has P(X_1 + X_2 > x) ~ 2 F̄(x), by definition. It includes the lognormal law and the Weibull law with k < 1, which are not regularly varying.
proof: The lower bound: {max X_i > x} ⊂ {S_n > x} when the X_i are positive, and P(max X_i > x) = 1 − F(x)^n ~ n F̄(x). The upper bound for n = 2: if X_1 + X_2 > x, then X_1 > (1 − ε)x, or X_2 > (1 − ε)x, or both are above εx. The first two events have probability at most 2 F̄((1 − ε)x) ~ 2(1 − ε)^(−α) F̄(x). The third has probability F̄(εx)², which is o(F̄(x)). Let ε → 0. Induction on n gives the general case.
reference: P. Embrechts, C. Klüppelberg and T. Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events for Insurance and Finance, Springer, 1997, section 1.3 and appendix A3. N. H. Bingham, C. M. Goldie and J. L. Teugels, Regular Variation, Cambridge University Press, 1987.
counterexample: For the standard exponential law, P(X_1 + X_2 > x) = (1 + x) e^(−x), so the ratio to 2 P(X > x) is (1 + x)/2 → ∞. A large sum of light-tailed values comes from many moderate values, not from one large value.

title: Extreme-value limits and domains of attraction
statement: \begin{gathered} \mathbb{P}\left(\frac{M_n - b_n}{a_n} \le x\right) = F(a_n x + b_n)^n \to G(x) \ \text{non-degenerate} \ \Longrightarrow \\ G(x) = \exp\left(-(1 + \xi x)^{-1/\xi}\right), \ 1 + \xi x > 0, \ \text{for some} \ \xi \in \mathbb{R} \end{gathered}
assumptions: M_n is the maximum of n i.i.d. values with the law F, and a_n > 0 and b_n are constants.
G is non-degenerate: it is not a point mass. Then G is a GEV law, up to a change of location and scale (Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko).

Domains of attraction: ξ > 0 if and only if F̄ is regularly varying with index 1/ξ. ξ < 0 if and only if the end point x_F is finite and F̄(x_F − 1/x) is regularly varying with index −1/ξ. ξ = 0 holds for laws such as the normal, exponential, Gompertz and lognormal laws.
proof: Max-stability: let F^n(a_n x + b_n) → G. Then for each k, the maximum of k blocks of n values gives G^k(α_k x + β_k) = G(x). By the convergence of types (Khinchine), G is max-stable. Take logarithms: −log G is a positive decreasing function that satisfies a Cauchy-type functional equation. Its only solutions are (1 + ξx)^(−1/ξ) and e^(−x) (the case ξ = 0).
reference: P. Embrechts, C. Klüppelberg and T. Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events for Insurance and Finance, Springer, 1997, theorems 3.2.3 and 3.3.7. L. de Haan and A. Ferreira, Extreme Value Theory: An Introduction, Springer, 2006, theorem 1.1.3. S. Coles, An Introduction to Statistical Modeling of Extreme Values, Springer, 2001, chapter 3.
counterexample: The Poisson law is in no domain of attraction. P(X = k)/P(X ≥ k) does not tend to 0, so no constants a_n and b_n give a non-degenerate limit of its maxima. The geometric law has the same problem. A discrete law needs this jump condition before the theorem can apply.

title: Threshold exceedances, maxima and sums
statement: \begin{gathered} F \in \mathrm{MDA}(G_\xi) \iff \lim_{u \to x_F} \ \sup_{0 < y < x_F - u} \left| \mathbb{P}(X - u \le y \mid X > u) - H_{\xi, \sigma(u)}(y) \right| = 0 \\ H_{\xi,\sigma}(y) = 1 - (1 + \xi y/\sigma)^{-1/\xi}, \qquad \text{for } X \sim H_{\xi,\sigma}: \ \mathbb{E}[X - u \mid X > u] = \frac{\sigma + \xi u}{1 - \xi} \ (\xi < 1) \end{gathered}
assumptions: X has the law F with the upper end point x_F, which can be ∞.
F is in the maximum domain of attraction of the GEV law G_ξ, for a suitable function σ(u) > 0 (Pickands–Balkema–de Haan).
The GPD H_ξ,σ is threshold stable: its excess over u is GPD with the same ξ and the scale σ + ξu. Thus its mean excess is linear in u for ξ < 1.
proof: Take logarithms of F^n(a_n x + b_n) → G_ξ(x): n F̄(a_n x + b_n) → (1 + ξx)^(−1/ξ). Divide the value at x + y by the value at x. Put u = a_n x + b_n. Then F̄(u + a_n y)/F̄(u) → (1 + ξy/(1 + ξx))^(−1/ξ). This is the GPD survival function with the scale σ(u) = a_n(1 + ξx). Monotonicity of F̄ makes the convergence uniform in y.
reference: A. A. Balkema and L. de Haan, Residual life time at great age, Annals of Probability 2 (1974) 792–804. J. Pickands, Statistical inference using extreme order statistics, Annals of Statistics 3 (1975) 119–131. P. Embrechts, C. Klüppelberg and T. Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events for Insurance and Finance, Springer, 1997, theorem 3.4.13.
counterexample: The theorem is a limit. At a fixed threshold the excess law of the lognormal law is not a GPD law. The lognormal law is in the domain ξ = 0, but its mean excess still increases with u. Thus a fit at a practical threshold often shows an apparent ξ > 0. The Poisson law, which is in no domain of attraction, has no GPD limit at all.

title: Ergodicity, mixing, and time and ensemble averages
statement: \begin{gathered} (X_n) \text{ irreducible, positive recurrent with stationary law } \pi: \quad \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(X_k) \to \sum_x \pi(x) f(x) \ \text{a.s. for every } X_0 \\ \text{and, if also aperiodic:} \quad \lVert P^n(x, \cdot) - \pi \rVert_{TV} \to 0 \end{gathered}
assumptions: The chain is irreducible: each state reaches each other state.
It is positive recurrent. A finite irreducible chain always is. Then the stationary law π is unique.
f has a finite mean under π. The convergence of the law Pⁿ(x, ·) needs aperiodicity. The convergence of the time average does not.
For a general stationary process, Birkhoff's theorem gives the limit E[f | invariant σ-field] of the time average. This limit equals the ensemble average when the process is ergodic.
proof: Split the path at the returns to a state x. The excursions between returns are i.i.d. (strong Markov property), and positive recurrence gives them a finite mean length E_x τ_x = 1/π(x). The strong law of large numbers applies to the sums of f over the excursions and to their lengths. The ratio of the two sums gives Σ π f. For the law, couple two copies of the chain, one started from π, until they meet at a time T. Aperiodicity and irreducibility make T finite, and ‖Pⁿ(x, ·) − π‖_TV ≤ P(T > n).
reference: J. R. Norris, Markov Chains, Cambridge University Press, 1997, theorems 1.8.3 and 1.10.2. D. A. Levin and Y. Peres, Markov Chains and Mixing Times, 2nd ed., American Mathematical Society, 2017, chapter 4. G. D. Birkhoff, Proof of the ergodic theorem, PNAS 17 (1931) 656–660.
counterexample: Geometric Brownian motion is not stationary. Let μ < σ²/2. Then (log S_t)/t → μ − σ²/2 < 0 almost surely, so almost every path tends to 0. But when μ > 0, the ensemble average E S_t = S_0 e^(μt) grows. The mean of many paths and the long-run growth of one path differ. A reducible chain with two closed classes also has a time average that depends on X_0.

title: Sklar's theorem and copulas
statement: \begin{gathered} F(x_1, \dots, x_d) = C\left(F_1(x_1), \dots, F_d(x_d)\right) \text{ for a copula } C, \text{ unique on } \operatorname{Ran} F_1 \times \dots \times \operatorname{Ran} F_d \\ U \sim C, \ X_j = F_j^{-1}(U_j) \ \Longrightarrow \ X \sim F, \qquad \tau, \ \lambda_U, \ \lambda_L \text{ depend on } C \text{ only} \end{gathered}
assumptions: F is a d-dimensional CDF with the margins F_1, …, F_d.
A copula is a CDF on [0, 1]^d with uniform margins.
C is unique when every margin is continuous. A discrete margin leaves C free outside the range of the margins, so discrete data do not identify their copula.
λ_U = lim_{q→1} P(U_2 > q | U_1 > q) and λ_L = lim_{q→0} P(U_2 ≤ q | U_1 ≤ q), where the limits exist.
proof: For continuous margins, U_j = F_j(X_j) is uniform, and C is the CDF of U. Then F(x) = P(U_j ≤ F_j(x_j) for all j) = C(F_1(x_1), …). Conversely, F_j^(−1)(U_j) ≤ x_j if and only if U_j ≤ F_j(x_j), so the quantile transform of U ~ C has the CDF C(F_1, …, F_d). Kendall's tau and the tail coefficients are invariant under strictly increasing maps of the components, so they depend only on C. For discrete margins, extend F by interpolation to a continuous CDF on the range.
reference: A. Sklar, Fonctions de répartition à n dimensions et leurs marges, Publ. Inst. Statist. Univ. Paris 8 (1959) 229–231. R. B. Nelsen, An Introduction to Copulas, 2nd ed., Springer, 2006, theorems 2.10.9 and 5.1.9. A. J. McNeil, R. Frey and P. Embrechts, Quantitative Risk Management, revised ed., Princeton University Press, 2015, chapter 7.
counterexample: The Gaussian and the Student t copula with the same correlation ρ = 0.5 have the same Kendall's tau, (2/π) arcsin ρ = 1/3. But λ_U = 0 for the Gaussian copula, and λ_U is about 0.25 for the t copula with ν = 4. The same margins and the same tau thus give different probabilities of joint extremes.

title: Multilevel Monte Carlo and discretisation bias
statement: \begin{gathered} |\mathbb{E}[P_l - P]| \le c_1 2^{-\alpha l}, \ V_l \le c_2 2^{-\beta l}, \ C_l \le c_3 2^{\gamma l}, \ \alpha \ge \tfrac12 \min(\beta, \gamma) \\ \Longrightarrow \ \exists L, N_l: \ \mathbb{E}\left[(\hat\theta - \mathbb{E}P)^2\right] < \varepsilon^2 \ \text{with cost} \ \le c_4 \begin{cases} \varepsilon^{-2} & \beta > \gamma \\ \varepsilon^{-2} (\log \varepsilon)^2 & \beta = \gamma \\ \varepsilon^{-2 - (\gamma - \beta)/\alpha} & \beta < \gamma \end{cases} \end{gathered}
assumptions: P_l is the quantity on the grid of level l, and P is its limit. The correction Y_l = P_l − P_(l−1) uses P_l and P_(l−1) on the same Brownian path.
The rates α, β and γ hold for every level. For the Euler–Maruyama scheme and a Lipschitz payoff, α = β = γ = 1.
The levels are independent, so the variance of the estimator is Σ V_l/N_l.
The mean square error is the sum of the Monte Carlo variance and the squared bias: E[(θ̂ − EP)²] = Σ V_l/N_l + (E P_L − E P)².
proof: Choose L with c_1 2^(−αL) ≤ ε/√2, so the squared bias is at most ε²/2. Minimise the cost Σ N_l C_l under the constraint Σ V_l/N_l ≤ ε²/2 with a Lagrange multiplier: N_l ∝ √(V_l/C_l). The cost is then 2ε^(−2)(Σ √(V_l C_l))². The sum Σ 2^((γ−β)l/2) stays bounded when β > γ, grows as L when β = γ, and grows as 2^((γ−β)L/2) when β < γ. With L ≈ log2(1/ε)/α this gives the three cases.
reference: M. B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo path simulation, Operations Research 56 (2008) 607–617. M. B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, theorem 1. P. E. Kloeden and E. Platen, Numerical Solution of Stochastic Differential Equations, Springer, 1992, chapters 10 and 14.
counterexample: Take the indicator that Brownian motion reaches a level, checked only at the grid times. A fine and a coarse path disagree with a probability of order 2^(−l/2), so β = 1/2 < γ = 1. The cost then grows as ε^(−3) up to a log factor, near the cost of plain Monte Carlo. The interval of a plain run on one grid also says nothing about its bias: a smaller interval does not reduce the monitoring bias.
